title: Diwan Todar Mal
hookLine: tradition says he bought land for the children's cremation by covering it with gold coins

lines: A PRICE MEANT TO SEND HIM AWAY.
cards: Sirhind, in winter. The sentence has been carried out. The Guru's two youngest sons, Zorawar Singh and Fateh Singh, are dead, and tradition says their grandmother, Mata Gujri, died in the cold tower.
Now a family is owed one more thing: a cremation. That takes ground, and the ground around Sirhind belongs to people who are afraid of the governor. Nobody wants to be the one who helped.
Then a man of the town with wealth and position steps forward and asks to buy a plot. Tradition says the owner named a price meant to make him leave. Today: Diwan Todar Mal.

teach.b: Here is the price, as tradition tells it. The owner would sell only as much ground as Todar Mal could cover with gold coins.

Some tellings go further: the coins had to stand on their edges, side by side, so the cost would be far higher than coins laid flat. Either way, it was an outrageous demand, and Todar Mal didn't bargain.
He brought the gold, covered the ground, and bought it. Mata Gujri and the two boys were cremated there with dignity.
Sikhs remember the spot at Fatehgarh Sahib, where a gurdwara now stands, and they gather there in winter to remember the children. Three things here are worth slowing down for. First, who he was.
Todar Mal was not a Sikh soldier or a member of the Guru's household.

teach.h: NOT A SIKH, AND HE RISKED IT ALL.
teach.b: Sikh tradition remembers him as a Hindu of Sirhind, a man with position and wealth to lose, and he risked both.
Second, who the gift was for: people who could never repay it, a grandmother and two children who had already died. Third, what the gold bought.
Not a monument, not a statement, just enough ground to do what a family is owed. Grief, in this story, becomes something practical. Nobody could undo the sentence.

teach.h: THE ONE THING STILL LEFT TO DO.
teach.b: Todar Mal did the one thing still left to do, and he did it at full price.
Sikhs remember his name with deep gratitude, as a reminder that the person who stands closest in the hardest hour can be a neighbor with a purse and a conscience.

how: Sikhs remember Diwan Todar Mal at Fatehgarh Sahib, where Mata Gujri and the younger Sahibzade were cremated, and gather there in winter to honor the children and those who stood by them.

practice: Bring to mind one cause that serves people who can't pay you back: a food bank, a hospice, a gurdwara's langar, a family on your street going through a loss.
Picture the gift you could give, money, time or something you own, and notice the urge to bargain it down. Let the first, larger number stand.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: Diwan Todar Mal; Diwan is the title he is remembered by.
